reasoning: Both sets are detailed, ID-linked plans with a walking-skeleton first milestone, an interface phase, spine/wiring/system phases and context packets. Neither matches the user's facts exactly: both use SSE where the user asked for WebSocket, and both use the nasdaq-data-link client rather than Sharadar's own API. Set A covers the user's four stages more fully. It has one shared walk-forward engine with gaps and a held-back lockbox, a hypothesis ledger that routes every claim through null-hypothesis-testing, PCA factors fitted per window, Marchenko–Pastur denoising, a covariance ranking, classical portfolios stored as the S4 benchmark, and S4 with neural forecasters, PPO agents under a configuration budget and rented-GPU bundles. It also has 27 golden cases in M1, a single interface task that freezes all three packages with fakes for calls between pipelines, and spines that each depend only on that interface task. Set A's weak points are concrete. It has no Yahoo/yahooquery cross-check and never uses the user's list of 10 delisted names. CONSTRAINTS.md is missing, although every packet tells the builder to read it. Reference files are not assigned to milestones in the roadmap. S3 tests features by rank correlation only, with no ML step. Set B handles S1 validation better: it has a Yahoo cross-check (though through yfinance, not yahooquery), a CHECK-09 test on the 10 delisted names, references placed on milestones, ideas files and a full CONSTRAINTS.md. But it removes the PPO agents and the rented GPU from S4, which the user asked for. Its data, server and app packages have no golden cases at all. It also has stale labels (spines marked 'Kind: thicken', '(new)' on files an earlier task already wrote), an unverified $49 Sharadar line counted against the $50 budget for other sources, and three interface tasks that run in parallel while importing from each other. On balance Set A's stage coverage, test oracles and interface discipline outweigh Set B's better S1 cross-check.
